events.reader:
Selected audience: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs.
Situation context (grounded; check applicability): This is an ops/IT-adjacent person at a company where policies and handbooks are written up in Notion or similar docs and employees communicate primarily in Slack; when someone can't find an answer, they ping this person (or the team channel) directly, and this person has been asked to build or is considering building an automated Slack responder that draws on the Handbook, Docs, and Issue Trackers.
events.reader_segment: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs
events.promise: You can have an answer-bot live in Slack over your own handbook documents — configured, not assembled — and see, run by run, which document it answered from and what it cost.
events.arc: Single email. It opens on the request this reader already has in their queue — an automated responder in the questions channel — names what standing that up actually involves today, then announces that the assembly step is now the product: documents in, Slack out, every answer logged. It closes on the smallest possible first move: one agent, one document set, one channel, tested before anyone else sees it.

emails.job: Get an ops/IT generalist to sign up and stand up one agent over one set of their own handbook documents, connected to Slack, and look at the first runs.
emails.single_idea: orqAgent is live: the Slack answer-bot over your handbook is now a configuration rather than a build — you point it at your documents, install it in Slack, and every answer it gives is a logged run you can open up.
emails.objection: If we open this to the whole company, what does it actually cost us — and would I even know before the bill arrives?
must_not_say: No plan names, prices, credit counts, execution or run limits, and no '55 Sonnet calls' style equivalences — the company's two published pricing tables contradict each other on the Pro plan and on free-tier runs, and a number the reader can disprove in one click costs more than it buys. The next step is the sign-up page; let the page carry the terms.

No claim or implication that retrieval is semantic or embedding-based, and no claim about answer accuracy, deflection rate or hours saved. Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks; the honest move is to invite the reader to test it on their own documents, never to assert quality.

No uptime, SLA, SOC 2, encryption, GDPR or security-posture claims. SOC 2 is only in progress, the uptime guarantee is Enterprise-only, and this reader is not running a vendor security review yet — raising it starts a conversation the evidence cannot finish.

No competitor names and no comparison on speed, breadth, model coverage, quality, effort, control or security. The field is ahead of us on every one of those axes; the email loses the moment it invites the comparison.
No customer names, logos, testimonials, user counts, funding or founding story — none exist in the material, and inventing warmth here is the one failure that cannot be repaired later.

Do not state that this reader has already built a bot, already abandoned one, already has a tool in place, or that their documentation runs to any particular length. Their situation is that questions keep coming and a responder has been asked for or considered — keep the build in the conditional ('if you've priced out wiring this yourself').

Do not position this as replacing a workspace AI assistant or knowledge base the company may already pay for. There is nothing in the material that answers 'why add a third thing', so the ask is 'run one agent beside what exists', never 'switch'.
Do not promise voice or telephony support, or imply the agent replaces a backend, product UI, billing or an operational workflow.
Do not present guardrails, per-client agent configuration, HIPAA compliance or deep domain-specific operational integrations as available capabilities.
Do not name a dollar figure per answer or per month. Spend is tracked and visible; that is the claim. Converting tracked spend into a forecast the reader can hold us to is not.
No hype vocabulary — no 'revolutionary', 'game-changing', 'cutting-edge', 'leverage', or 'solution'. This company writes in short declarative sentences with a concrete follow-up after an em dash.
Do not promise voice or telephony support unless a current licensed source explicitly establishes it.
Do not claim that the agent layer replaces a company's complete backend, product UI, billing, or operational workflow without direct evidence.
Compliance and certification claims are unavailable unless the Evidence Ledger explicitly licenses them.
Do not claim Knowledge base / RAG context; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Agent guardrails; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Reusable per-client agent configuration; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Voice and telephony runtime; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim Full SaaS backend replacement; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim HIPAA compliance; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Deep domain-specific operational integrations; its capability state is unknown.

Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks (E56, E57) rather than semantic search, and the free tier caps the knowledge base at five documents (E120), so a question worded unlike the handbook or spread across a large page.

The 99.9% uptime figure is only contractually guaranteed on Enterprise (E147, E37), Starter keeps just 7 days of run history and Pro 30 days of analytics (E28, E32), and hitting the monthly quota returns a hard 429 (E129).
emails.felt_need: The same policy and handbook questions get asked repeatedly in Slack, and the answers are buried in documentation that is difficult to navigate.
emails.status_quo: Team members search Notion by trying random keywords or guessing document titles rather than getting a direct answer.
emails.why_it_fails: That assembly is on record as a fast way to prototype and a poor fit for what this ends up being — a high-scale, latency-sensitive thing the whole company uses, needing observability and reliability the orchestration layer was not built to give. And once it exists, it is a running system with no owner.
emails.mechanism: The pieces stop being yours to assemble: documents are uploaded and the relevant context is retrieved for every query with no vector database to run, Slack is a native OAuth install where the bot answers mentions and channel messages, and latency, token usage per model and daily spend are tracked automatically with no extra configuration — so the thing you would have had to build the monitoring for arrives already monitored.

events.body:
orqAgent is live. You can now stand up an agent over your own handbook documents and put it in Slack, where it answers the policy questions that keep coming back to you.

Those answers usually exist already, written up in Notion or somewhere like it. Finding one means guessing at keywords and document titles until something turns up — which is why the question comes to you instead.

If you have priced out wiring this yourself — Slack events, a store to search, a model API — the prototype is the quick part. What follows is a production system the whole company uses, and it has no owner.

Here that assembly is configuration. Upload PDFs, docs or plain text; the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query, with no vector DB to manage. Slack is an OAuth install — the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

Before you open it to the whole company, the usage is visible while it runs: token usage per model, P95 latency and **daily spend trends**, tracked automatically without extra configuration.

Point one agent at one set of policy documents, connect a single channel, and read the first runs.
events.postscript: Your first agent takes under two minutes to create, and no card is required.

edits.line: What follows is a production system the whole company uses, and it has no owner.
edits.problem: This is the line all three readers cut and where two of them stopped. It asserts as settled fact a future the audience profile does not establish — company-wide scale and an ownership burden — and it converts the brief's limitation beat into a scare about what the reader's own build would become rather than naming work they would have to keep doing. Arriving after a paragraph that already opened in the conditional, it reads as the email telling the reader what their situation is.
edits.fix: Keep the limitation inside the conditional the paragraph already opened, and confine it to concrete work the reader would own and maintain (the Slack events, the store, the model API, and the monitoring on top). Drop the assertion of a company-wide production system and the ownerless-system dramatization, and reach the configuration paragraph sooner.

edits.line: Before you open it to the whole company, the usage is visible while it runs: token usage per model, P95 latency and daily spend trends, tracked automatically without extra configuration.
edits.problem: The ask is one agent on one channel, but this clause makes company-wide deployment the assumed destination. That is precisely the frame all three readers said stops the click — an unknown vendor answering HR policy questions for everyone — and the email has no licensed material on security, data handling, accuracy or uptime with which to finish that conversation. The email raises the hardest objection about itself and then walks past it.
edits.fix: Attach the visibility to the small test actually being asked for — a single agent on a single channel, watched run by run — so the observability benefit lands without opening a rollout question the evidence cannot close.

edits.line: Point one agent at one set of policy documents, connect a single channel, and read the first runs.
edits.problem: "Read the first runs" (and the preview text's "read the runs it logs") is the email's whole answer to its assigned objection — would I know what this costs before the bill arrives — yet nothing on the page says what a run actually shows. Two readers filled that silence with the question they cared about instead: does it tell me which document the answer came from. The campaign promise claims per-run document attribution that the evidence does not license, so the copy cannot answer that; what it can do is stop leaving the run undefined.
edits.fix: Make one concrete statement of what the reader sees in a run, using only what evidence supports — the per-run estimated cost recorded with the run (E73), and the tracked latency, token usage per model and daily spend (E12). Keep the cost figure scoped to the run record, not to something that appears beside the Slack reply, and do not imply source-document citation.

edits.problem: The captured voice has no greetings and no individual signature; the company opens straight into what the thing does. "Hi there" is generic mail-merge and was one of the first lines a reader cut, and it softens an announcement whose confidence comes from describing something that already exists.
edits.fix: Open on the announcement itself. Let "orqAgent is live" carry the first line and keep the plain team sign-off.

edits.problem: The pivot from problem to product rests on an abstract noun swap that asks the reader to hold two earlier paragraphs in mind to decode "that assembly." The company's rhythm is a plain claim followed by a literal follow-up; this is the one sentence in the email that sounds like a competent stranger.
edits.fix: State plainly what the reader does instead, in the same concrete register as the sentences that follow it, without the abstract restatement.

events.body:
An answer-bot over your handbook is now something you configure, not something you build.

orqAgent is **now available**. You point one agent at your own handbook documents, connect it to Slack, and every answer it gives is a logged run.

The answers already exist, written up in Notion or somewhere like it. Finding one means guessing at keywords and page titles, which is why the question lands with you instead.

If you have sketched out wiring this yourself — Slack events, a store to search, a model API — the prototype is the quick part. The monitoring on top is yours to write and to keep working.

Upload PDFs, docs or plain text; the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query, with no vector DB to manage. Slack is an OAuth install — the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

Each message it handles is recorded as a run carrying **an estimated USD cost**, and P95 latency, token usage per model and daily spend trends are tracked automatically, without extra configuration.

Start with one agent, one set of policy documents, one channel — and read what comes back.
events.postscript: Creating the first agent takes under two minutes, and no card is required.
